markdown_block.answer:
TCP and QUIC pursue the same fundamental objective—adapt sending rate to available network capacity and back off on congestion—but QUIC makes loss recovery and congestion signaling more explicit at the transport layer. Its default controller is broadly NewReno-like, so the most consequential differences are usually in **the feedback and recovery machinery around the controller**, not simply “QUIC uses a completely different congestion algorithm.” QUIC implementations may also use alternative controllers such as CUBIC, subject to Internet congestion-control guidelines.[1]

## At a glance

| Dimension | TCP | QUIC |
|---|---|---|
| Data and packet identity | TCP numbers **bytes**; retransmissions reuse the same byte sequence numbers, creating ambiguity about whether an ACK covers an original transmission or retransmission. [2] | Every transmitted QUIC packet gets a new, strictly increasing packet number within its packet-number space; retransmitted data is placed into a *new* packet. That removes retransmission ambiguity. [1] |
| ACK information | TCP ACKs are fundamentally cumulative: an ACK says the next byte expected. SACK is an optional extension, and TCP has limited option-header space. [2] | ACK frames natively carry received packet ranges—similar in purpose to SACK—and QUIC supports more ACK ranges than TCP’s three SACK blocks. QUIC ACKs cannot be “reneged” after acknowledgment. [1] |
| Loss detection | Classic TCP fast retransmit treats three duplicate ACKs as a loss signal; timeouts are handled through retransmission timeout (RTO) logic. [3] | QUIC declares a packet lost based on packet-threshold or time-threshold evidence after a later packet is acknowledged. The recommended initial packet-reordering threshold is three packets; the recommended time threshold is \(9/8\) of the larger of smoothed and latest RTT. [1] |
| Timeout response | Under the RFC 5681 TCP behavior, an RTO loss reduces `cwnd` to one full-sized segment and restarts with slow start. [3] | QUIC uses a Probe Timeout (PTO) to send one or two ACK-eliciting probes. A PTO by itself does **not** mark packets lost or collapse `cwnd`; QUIC collapses the window only upon persistent congestion. [1] |
| RTT measurement | TCP’s cumulative ACK model can make distinguishing original versus retransmitted segments difficult; timestamps can help. [2] | QUIC takes RTT samples using newly acknowledged largest packet numbers and explicitly accounts for peer-reported ACK delay, bounded by the peer’s declared maximum ACK delay after handshake confirmation. [1] |
| Handshake/recovery state | TCP’s SYN/SYN-ACK loss is treated specially in classic congestion-control behavior. [1] | QUIC maintains separate packet-number spaces for Initial, Handshake, and application traffic (with 0-RTT and 1-RTT sharing one space). Loss detection is separate by space, reducing cross-phase ambiguity; congestion control and RTT estimation remain unified per path. [1] |
| Minimum congestion window | Classic TCP’s minimum congestion window is one packet. [1] | QUIC recommends two packets, to reduce the chance that losing a lone in-flight packet forces a lengthy timeout recovery. [1] |
| ACK-only packets | TCP ACK behavior is typically not part of the sender’s congestion window. | QUIC likewise excludes ACK-only packets from bytes in flight and congestion control, but can detect their loss and may use that information to adjust behavior. [1] |

## The key conceptual difference

A useful simplification is:

> **TCP congestion control is historically coupled to a byte-stream protocol with cumulative acknowledgments; QUIC congestion control is built around explicit packet-level transmission history.**

TCP provides reliable, in-order **byte-stream** delivery. Its standard ACK indicates the next byte expected, meaning it cumulatively confirms everything before that point; SACK adds information about some received ranges but is optional and constrained by TCP’s option format.[2]

QUIC treats packets as distinct transmissions. If a STREAM frame is lost, QUIC does not “retransmit packet 123”; it sends the necessary frame again in a later packet with a **new** packet number. Consequently, when an ACK says packet 145 arrived, the sender knows exactly which transmission succeeded. That makes loss inference, spurious-loss detection, and RTT sampling less ambiguous.[1]

This difference matters most on mobile, Wi‑Fi, or other paths with reordering, short bursts, and tail loss—conditions in which distinguishing “lost,” “late,” and “retransmitted” packets is important.

## Loss and recovery behavior

### TCP: duplicate ACKs and RTOs

The classic TCP model standardized in RFC 5681 has four interrelated mechanisms:

- Slow start
- Congestion avoidance
- Fast retransmit
- Fast recovery[3]

When a TCP sender receives three duplicate ACKs, it treats that as an indication that a segment was likely lost and retransmits it without waiting for a timer. It lowers the slow-start threshold to at most half the outstanding flight size and enters fast recovery.[3]

If a retransmission timeout fires, TCP responds much more conservatively: it sets `cwnd` to one segment and returns to slow start.[3]

Modern operating systems commonly deploy more advanced TCP mechanisms—such as SACK-based recovery, RACK, CUBIC, or BBR—so real TCP behavior can differ substantially from the classic RFC 5681 baseline. But the baseline is important for understanding the contrast drawn by QUIC’s standard recovery specification.[2][3]

### QUIC: packet/time thresholds and PTO

QUIC uses ACK feedback to evaluate whether each outstanding packet is:

- Acknowledged
- Lost by packet threshold
- Lost by time threshold
- Still in flight[1]

A packet can be declared lost when a later packet has been acknowledged and the earlier packet is sufficiently behind in packet number or time. This is conceptually similar to modern TCP loss-recovery designs, but QUIC’s packet numbering makes the evidence clearer.[1]

QUIC’s PTO is particularly important. It is calculated roughly as:

\[
\text{PTO} = \text{smoothed RTT} + \max(4 \cdot \text{RTT variation}, \text{timer granularity}) + \text{max ACK delay}
\]

On PTO expiration, QUIC probes for feedback—normally by sending at least one ACK-eliciting packet, and possibly two full-sized datagrams. It does not automatically decide prior packets were lost or reduce the congestion window solely because the PTO expired.[1]

That distinction prevents a single tail loss or lost ACK from being treated as conclusive evidence of sustained congestion. QUIC instead applies its strongest window collapse when it detects **persistent congestion**, while still exponentially backing off PTO intervals if consecutive probes fail.[1]

## Congestion-window behavior

Both protocols use a sender-side congestion window (`cwnd`) and usually react to loss or ECN congestion signals by cutting their sending allowance. QUIC’s specified baseline is analogous to TCP NewReno: it has slow start, recovery, and congestion avoidance, and on a newly detected congestion event reduces the congestion window by about half.[1]

The practical divergence is the treatment of timeouts:

- **TCP RTO:** classic TCP treats timeout-detected loss as severe enough to reset `cwnd` to one segment.[3]
- **QUIC PTO:** the expiration itself is only an uncertainty/liveness event. QUIC sends probes and preserves `cwnd` unless it obtains evidence of persistent congestion.[1]

QUIC’s minimum `cwnd` recommendation of two packets instead of TCP’s one is another recovery-oriented design choice. It reduces the risk that the sender must wait for a timer after losing its sole in-flight packet, at the cost of allowing a modestly larger minimum amount of traffic.[1]

## What this means in practice

For an implementation engineer, QUIC often offers a cleaner substrate for modern congestion control:

- **More precise feedback:** Native ACK ranges and unique packet numbers expose which transmissions arrived.
- **Cleaner retransmission semantics:** Reliable data is retransmitted as a new packet, rather than creating ambiguity around the original packet’s sequence-number space.
- **Better tail-loss handling:** PTO probes can restore feedback without automatically collapsing sending rate.
- **More accurate RTT accounting:** ACK delay is explicitly reported and can be subtracted within protocol limits.
- **Per-path control:** QUIC defines congestion control per path, an especially relevant property when connections migrate between networks.[1]

But QUIC is not inherently “more aggressive” or automatically faster. A QUIC sender still must be congestion-controlled, and its actual throughput depends heavily on the chosen algorithm, pacing, ACK policy, path MTU, network loss/reordering, endpoint implementation, and middlebox behavior. QUIC’s advantage is principally that it gives the sender cleaner and richer signals for making those decisions.[1]

## Further knowledge

- [RFC 9002: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002.html) — The primary QUIC recovery and congestion-control specification; especially Sections 4, 6, and 7.[1]
- [RFC 5681: TCP Congestion Control](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5681.html) — The classic TCP slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, and fast recovery baseline.[3]
- [RFC 9293: Transmission Control Protocol](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293.html) — The current consolidated TCP base specification, including TCP’s byte-sequence and cumulative-ACK model.[2]
